doc.title: Michael Weiss interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 22, 2021

title: Coming to New York: playing with idols, not collecting records
summary: He had no plan beyond playing with admired players and rising through the ranks as a sideman; he is not a record completist.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Right. Well said. When you moved to New York in the early 80s, were you a goal-type person? Had you laid out a plan for what you hoped would happen?

No. I’m a little too disorganized for that. I mean to have this sort of, I’m pretty much a more spontaneous type of person, however, I did know that I wanted to play, I got the most gratification from playing with great players, players that I admired, players that I looked up to. I aspired to play with the players that I used to listen to on records that were in New York. I got great satisfaction out of being able to be on the bandstand and to be making music with my idols. And that was the type of career path that I guess I wanted to have. I wanted to come up through the ranks so to speak, because that was what I saw through all my recordings, sidemen who gained more and more appearances on recordings and became leaders in their own right, who established a track record, credentials — professional credentials — and I thought that’s the way I wanted my career to progress.

I see a collection of LPs behind you. And I know I used to spend many hours reading liner notes and almost like keeping track of how many LPs does Clark Terry show up on? And that kind of thing. And I wondered if you did that and did you envision some day seeing your name?

No. I didn’t really think like that. I’m not — I have a lot of records here but I’m not really a real record collector. I’m not a completist, you know. I have a lot of Jackie McLean records but I don’t have them all. I have a lot of records of particular artists but there are some that I don’t have that maybe a lot of people have in their collections, I just didn’t get around to it. I never really — I never really thought of like, okay one day I’m going to have a hit record, I’m going to do everything I can to be a Blue Note recording artist. I was just happy playing with great players and being able to tour with them. That was a sort of a mark of arrival, a confirmation that I’m doing what I set out to do.
